name: Grist
description: Osric Pennywort's wheel has been turning with no water since the night the Toll hummed. Go and look in the wheel-pit, and decide what to do about what is turning it.
notes: Stage numbers are 1-based. Branching: the choice option's quest_stage jumps to a branch stage (4 or 5); the branch stage's on_complete quest_stage rejoins at stage 6. 'leave' jumps straight to 6.

stages.journal: Osric Pennywort's wheel has been turning with no water since the night the Toll hummed. He is grinding with it, because flour is flour, and his daughter will not go near the mill, and he would like someone who is not him to go and look in the wheel-pit.

The mill is a quarter-hour up the Larkbourne. The sluice has been dry since the summer the stream moved; the wheel turns anyway, slow and steady, with a sound like somebody walking. Osric mentions, without meeting your eye, that this is the spare wheel: the good one was taken down to the Gosling Pit by the Larkbourne Boys and is a table now. The wheel-pit is under the floor, through the trap by the stones.

In the pit, under the wheel, an old man in a miller's apron is treading the paddles like a mill-horse, round and round, with his tools on his belt. He does not stop when you speak. He does not look up. The wheel turns because he turns it. Osric's grandfather was buried with his tools sixty years ago, in the yard, under the apple. You can put him to rest, which will stop the mill. You can leave him to it. Or you can find the old sluice pin, which Osric says his father threw in the Larkbourne's head-pool under the Hound the day the stream moved, and give the wheel back its water, and see whether the old man stops when the work is done.

options.text: Put him to rest. He has done enough.
Find the sluice pin. Give him back the water and see if he stops.

stages.journal: He will not stop for words. He will stop for what stops a hedge-wight. He has huge poise and a scythe he has not put down in sixty years; keep out of the sweep and hit him when he turns the corner of the pit. When he goes down the wheel will go on a few turns by itself and then stop.

The Larkbourne rises in a pool under the Chalk Hound's forepaw. The pin has been in the pool for a lifetime; oak lasts under water. Set it in the old sluice gate at the mill and lift the gate. If the old man is doing this because the work is not finished, water may finish it.

Tell Osric what is turning his wheel, and what you did about it. He will want to know whether it hurt. He will not want to know whether the flour was ever safe, so do not tell him unless he asks twice.

name: Seventeen Bells
description: One of Merrowby's seventeen family bells has gone silent. Find out whether any Fennick still lives, and decide whether the bell stays up, comes down, or goes south.
notes: Stage numbers are 1-based. Branching: 'give' jumps to stage 4 then rejoins at 5; 'keep' and 'bury' jump straight to 5.

stages.journal: Hesta Hollins keeps the seventeen small bells in Merrowby's trees, one for each family. The Fennick bell has stopped: it does not ring in wind or in the hand, and she has polished it every morning since spring. Custom says a bell for a family that is gone comes down at the Long Table and is buried in the crater. Aud Fennick, the last of them, put on grey and walked south to Cinderlea. If Aud lives, the bell stays up, even silent. Hesta would like to know which, and would rather not know it from the bell.

Pilgrims who go south stop at Pilgrim's Ash, where the Tolling Order feeds them and does not argue with them. If Aud Fennick is still on this side of the Hushline, she will be there, in grey, mending other people's grey.

Aud Fennick is alive, thin, and cheerful about it. She says the bell stopped when she stopped answering to the name, which she did on purpose, and that Hesta should take it down and sleep. Then she says that if it came south with her she would take it into the grey and it could be silent somewhere it mattered. Then she says to do as you like; she has stopped telling people what to do. You could tell Hesta the truth and let the bell hang; carry the bell to Aud; or tell Hesta the Fennicks are gone and let her bury it.

options.text: Tell Hesta that Aud lives. The bell stays up, silent or not.
Carry the bell south to Aud. Let her take it into the grey.
Tell Hesta the Fennicks are gone. Let her bury it and sleep.

stages.journal: Hesta will give you the Fennick bell if you tell her where it is going; she will not like it, and she will give it to you anyway, wrapped in the blue cuff. Carry it to Aud at Pilgrim's Ash. It will not ring on the way. Aud says it may ring on the other side, and that she will listen for it.

Go back to the bell trees and tell Hesta what you found and what you did. She will be at the trees at dawn with the cuff, whichever it was. Merrowby will have sixteen bells or seventeen by the Long Table, and the village will count them, because it counts everything.

name: Bramble
description: The smith's boy has lost his dog on the downs, where the down wolves hunt. Find Bramble, deal with the wolves, and decide what to carry home.
notes: Stage numbers are 1-based. Branching: 'nell' jumps to stage 5 and rejoins at 6; 'home' and 'end' jump straight to 6.

stages.journal: Robin Ashdown's dog Bramble went over the down after a hare two days ago and did not come back. Robin whistles for him at the top of every hour. Hallam says wolves have been heard in the dry valley below the Chalk Hound and that the boy is not to go, which is why the boy is asking you.

The Chalk Hound is cut into the down south of the village, white on green, big enough that you can lie in its eye. Robin says Bramble likes the eye because it is warm. Go up and look; take the hare-path, not the road. Mind the chalk pit below the Hound where the Larkbourne Boys camp, and listen for the wolves before they listen for you.

Bramble is in the Hound's eye, lying on his side with a hind leg wrong, thumping his tail at you. Three down wolves are circling the eye at a distance, lean and grey-gold, waiting for him to stop thumping it. They lunge when you turn your back. Do not turn your back.

The wolves are dealt with and the dog is still thumping his tail. The leg is broken and he is thin and he has been here two days. You can carry him straight home to Robin and hope. You can carry him first to Nell Harebell, who mends things and charges for it. Or you can end it here, quickly, and take him the collar, which is what Hallam would do and what Hallam would never forgive himself for.

options.text: Carry him home to Robin now.
Carry him to Nell Harebell first.
End it. Take the collar home.

stages.journal: Nell Harebell's stillroom is behind the hives. She will set the leg and splint it with hazel and say the dog will limp and live, in that order, and she will want paying, because kindness that is not paid for goes quiet. Fifteen marks or something from the downs she can use.
Take what you are carrying to Robin. He will be on the green, or at the forge watching his father, or at the well with Winnow. He will hear you coming; he has been listening for two days.

name: Cask and Press
description: The Long Table wants one drink at the head of it, and Merrowby's brewer and Tamwick's orchard-keeper have wanted that place for twenty years. Taste, judge, broker, or tamper.
notes: Stage numbers are 1-based. Branching: 'sabotage' jumps to 4 then to 6; the three honest options jump to 5 then 6. The wassail option needs Speech 20.

stages.journal: Corwen Mullard would like you to go to Tamwick and 'look at' Bessa Tamwick's cider press before the Long Table, since it has a screw in it that he thinks wants tightening, and since a press without a screw is a table. He says this looking at his casks and not at you.

Tamwick is the orchard hamlet east along the down: the only apple trees in Wickmere and the only press. Bessa Tamwick will already know why you have come; Merrowby is not a place where a stranger walks east unremarked. She has a request of her own, which is that you taste both and say the truth at the Long Table, whichever way it falls.

You have tasted both. The ale is dark and honest and tastes of the cellar of a bell. The cider is sharp and gold and tastes of a tree that remembers eleven others. One goes at the head of the Long Table. You can say ale, or cider; you can try to talk them into a wassail of both, which nobody has managed in twenty years; or you can take the screw out of the press one night and let the question answer itself.

options.text: Take the screw. A press without a screw is a table.
Say ale at the Long Table, and mean it.
Say cider at the Long Table, and mean it.
Talk them into a wassail: both in one bowl, warmed.

stages.journal: The press screw is iron, worn bright by forty harvests, and heavy. Bessa sleeps in the press-house. Take it at night, and take it to Corwen, who will pay and will not ask how, and who will not sleep well either.
Tell Corwen what you will say at the Long Table. He has named a cask after you already; which end of the row it goes in depends on the next minute.
Go and tell Bessa. Whatever you did, she will hear of it by Tollday from somebody less kind, so it had better be from you first. The Grafted Tree is behind the press-house; she will be under it.

name: The Last Name of Mullbourne
description: Old Pellam says the names of three quiet hamlets to the Toll every dawn, and this week he could only find two. Find the third before it goes, and decide who should have it.
notes: Stage numbers are 1-based. Branching: 'tell' jumps to 5, 'strike' to 6, 'let_go' to 7; all rejoin at 8.

stages.journal: Pellam Ashcombe has said the names of the three quiet hamlets to the Toll every dawn for fifty years: Larkstead, Gosford, and a third. This week the third would not come. He stood at the rim with his mouth open and nothing in it. Wren says a name nobody can find is a weight and should be let go. Pellam says a name let go is a place that never was. He would like you to find it, and not to tell Wren you are looking.

Merrick Gosling once sang a verse about a wedding in a hamlet on soft ground, years back, and changed the name to make it scan. He may remember what he changed it from. He will certainly remember the wedding; the bride's sister married a Gullhithe eel-fisher, and Merrick has never forgiven the marsh for the quality of the ale.

Gullhithe is the eel-drying village on the north shore, under the Lamp. Tamsin Wick keeps the Lamp and turns the eels, and her mother's mother came from the soft-ground hamlet with an eel-knife that had the name on the handle. Tamsin has never said the name aloud to anyone who asked, because nobody has.

Mullbourne. Soft ground, a mill that never worked, nine households, a well that tasted of iron. Tamsin said it once and then looked as if she wanted it back. You can give it to Pellam, who will say it at dawn tomorrow and every dawn after. You can give it to Wren, who will re-ink the line on the Roll and then, by the Wardens' custom for names nobody living is tending, strike it through so that it cannot be lost again. Or you can tell Pellam you found nothing, and let him stop climbing to the rim in the dark.

options.text: Give the name to Pellam. Let him say it at dawn.
Give the name to Wren. Let the Wardens strike it clean.
Tell Pellam you found nothing. Let him rest.

stages.journal: Tell Pellam the name. He will make you say it twice, and then he will say it, and then he will be quiet for a while.

Tell Wren the name. She will write it into the Roll in fresh ink, read it aloud once so that it has been said by a Warden, and draw a line through it. She says a struck name is a mercy to the living who keep trying to remember. Pellam will not agree, and will not be told.

Tell Pellam there was nothing to find. He will believe you, because he wants to, and he will thank you, because he is polite. Tomorrow he will say two names at the rim, and the morning after that he may not climb up at all.
Sleep on it. In the morning, go to the rim at first light and listen to how many names Pellam says.

name: A Verse About You
description: Merrick Gosling has written verses about everyone in Merrowby except you. Give him a deed to hang one on, and decide what kind of verse it will be.
notes: Stage numbers are 1-based. The dialogue gates the offer on renown 40. Branching: 'brave' jumps to 3, 'kind' to 4, 'terrible' to 5; all rejoin at 6. The performance can be paid for grander in dialogue (flag verse_paid).

stages.journal: Merrick Gosling has a verse about everyone in Merrowby: Maud's oven, Hallam's one sword, the year Corwen's yellow door was painted blue overnight by persons unknown. He would like to write one about you now that people are saying your name, but a verse needs a deed to hang on, and he would like to choose the deed, or at least the kind of deed.

Merrick offers three hooks. A brave verse: the Larkbourne road has bandits on it again, five of them, and nobody remembers the Larkbourne Boys, which is exactly what they are counting on. A kind verse: Hesta Hollins has not had bread carried to her door since her husband died, because everyone assumes someone else does it. A terrible verse: the steward's brass key, taken from his belt in daylight, would be talked about for a year. He says all three sell.

options.text: Make it brave. Clear the Larkbourne road.
Make it kind. Carry bread to Hesta Hollins.
Make it terrible. Take the steward's key.

stages.journal: The Larkbourne Boys keep hall in the Tumbled Watch, a Warden tower lying on its side down a dry valley with its stair for a corridor. Five of them, and a caster on the fallen parapet. Come over the hilltop and you will see them before they see you. Merrick will want details, and will improve them.

Three hearth loaves from Maud's, carried warm to Hesta Hollins' door. Vale folk say a loaf carried to a neighbour counts as a sentence spoken. Three is a paragraph. Merrick says nobody has ever asked him for a kind verse and he is not sure he has the rhymes for it.

Ellard Wynstead polishes the brass key at the well at noon, in front of everybody, which is the point of it. Take it from his belt while he is doing so, or from the deed chest while he is not, and bring it to Merrick, who will not touch it and will describe it very well.

Merrick will sing it tonight at the Toll's Lip, at the hearth, after the second cask. He says the verse is finished and that it would be more finished for fifty marks, which would buy a third stanza in which you are taller.
